statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether the simple geometric visions seen on psychedelics come from spontaneous patterns of activity in the primary visual cortex (V1): a mathematical model proposes that they do, the paper tests it against no measurement in people on a drug (Bressloff et al., 2001), and no such test has been read for this answer. The model starts from Klüver's sorting of reported geometric hallucinations into four classes of 'form constants': gratings, lattices, fretworks, filigrees, honeycombs and chequer-boards; cobwebs; tunnels, funnels, alleys, cones and vessels; and spirals. The paper says such images are seen after flickering light, certain anaesthetics, deep pressure on the eyeballs, on waking or falling asleep, and shortly after drugs such as LSD and marijuana, and, citing earlier reports, that they are also seen by blind people and in sealed dark rooms and keep their positions relative to each other as the eyes move, so that they arise in the brain rather than the eyes. The model rests on the map from retina to V1, which away from the centre of gaze works like a complex logarithm, so that circles in the visual field fall on V1 as vertical lines, rays as horizontal lines and logarithmic spirals as oblique lines, making tunnels, funnels and spirals simple stripes of activity across V1; and on the wiring of V1, with cells tuned to the orientation of edges, connections within each local patch, and long lateral connections that link patches of the same orientation preference along the axis of that preference, measured mainly in cats, macaques, owl monkeys and tree shrews and scaled to human V1 (hypercolumns about 1.33 to 2 mm apart, about 1,300 per hemisphere); it extends an earlier model by the corresponding author and a colleague (Ermentrout & Cowan, 1979), which had no orientation tuning and could not produce lattice tunnels, honeycombs, some chequer-boards or cobwebs. When the model's resting state is made unstable, by raising excitability or lowering inhibition, which the authors describe as thought to be one possible effect of hallucinogens, a limited set of repeating patterns can arise: with weak inhibition between neighbouring orientation patches, light-and-dark patterns that map back to tunnels, funnels and spirals, and with strong inhibition, lattices of oriented edges that map back to honeycombs, chequer-boards and cobwebs. Its limits: the drug appears only as an abstract excitability setting, with no receptor, drug or dose, and the same mechanism is offered for flickering light; the match with hallucinations was judged by eye against a few drawings redrawn from secondary sources; the contour-forming patterns that match seen form constants needed lateral connections spreading more than 45 degrees from the orientation axis, wider than the anatomy that motivated the model, whose strict form gave patterns without continuous contours; the expected size of the patterns rests on an unsourced figure of 30 to 40 repetitions around the visual field (2.4 to 3.2 mm in V1); and some reported images, including a complex image after LSD, cannot be explained by the simple model, the authors say. The paper offers predictions, such as orientation changes detectable by optical imaging near the horizontal meridian, that it did not test. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Why do psychedelic visuals look like tunnels, spirals and honeycombs? A mathematical model suggests the visual brain's own wiring may shape them. The simple geometric visions people report, after LSD or cannabis but also with flickering light or on falling asleep, were sorted long ago into four types: lattices such as honeycombs and chequerboards, cobwebs, tunnels and funnels, and spirals. The wiring from the eye to the brain's first visual area turns a tunnel, a funnel or a spiral into simple stripes across that area. In the model, when the area becomes too excitable, stripes and lattices of activity form on their own, shaped by how its cells are connected, and mapped back to what a person would see they look like all four types. But it is only a model: the drug is just an excitability setting, the wiring was measured mostly in animals, the match was judged by eye against a few drawings, the best-matching patterns needed wider connections than the anatomy it was built on, and some complex visions do not fit it. The paper did not test it against brain activity measured in people on a drug.
population: No participants: a mathematical model of human primary visual cortex (V1), built from anatomical and physiological findings in cats, macaques, owl monkeys and tree shrews (partly unpublished, cited as personal communications) and from estimates of human V1 size and hypercolumn spacing, and compared with published drawings and descriptions of geometric hallucinations.
exposure: In the model, a rise in network excitability (stronger global coupling, or a steeper neural response through a steady input) or a fall in local inhibition, which the authors describe as one possible effect of hallucinogens and also apply to flickering light; no drug, receptor or dose is modelled.
comparator: The model's uniform resting state, and the earlier Ermentrout–Cowan model without orientation tuning; for the hallucinations, comparison by eye with a few drawings.
outcome: Which repeating (doubly periodic) patterns of V1 activity can emerge when the resting state becomes unstable, which of them are stable, and what they would look like in the visual field after an inverse retinocortical map; resemblance to Klüver's four classes of form constants, judged by eye.
magnitude: No statistical estimates. Retinocortical map constants w0 = 0.087 and epsilon = 0.051 (estimated from Drasdo, 1977); orientation preference repeating about every 300 µm in cat V1 and 0.5 mm in macaque V1; 20% of lateral connections ending on inhibitory cells; human V1 about 3,500 mm² per hemisphere, hypercolumn spacing about 1.33–2 mm, about 1,300 hypercolumns; critical wavelength given as about 2.66 mm (2π × 0.400 / qc at qc = 1 gives 2.51 mm, editors' calculation); 30–40 repetitions around the visual field for commonly reported hallucinations (unsourced), corresponding to 2.4–3.2 mm in V1; contour-forming (even) patterns need lateral spread beyond 45 degrees (theta0 > π/4).

evidence.locator: Abstract, 1st and 3rd paragraphs (p. 299) and last paragraph (p. 300)
evidence.extracted: The paper takes Klüver's four classes of form constants ((i) gratings, lattices, fretworks, filigrees, honeycombs and chequer-boards; (ii) cobwebs; (iii) tunnels, funnels, alleys, cones and vessels; (iv) spirals) and investigates mathematically the assumption that the retina-to-V1 map and V1's local and lateral circuits determine their geometry. It studies the patterns that emerge when the model's dynamics become unstable under the presumed action of hallucinogens or flickering lights and, given the authors' interpretation of the correspondence between V1 patterns and percepts, finds representatives of all the form constants; the results are sensitive to the detailed specification of the lateral connectivity, and the authors present a link to the processing of edges and contours as an interesting possibility if the mechanism is sited mainly in V1.

evidence.extracted: Orientation preference repeats about every 300 µm in cat V1 and about every 0.5 mm in macaque V1; cells less than 0.5 mm apart connect roughly isotropically, while long horizontal axons in layers II and III contact patches of similar orientation about every 0.5 mm along the axis of their orientation preference (owl monkey and tree shrew images, partly a personal communication); these come almost entirely from excitatory neurons, 20% ending on inhibitory cells. Some anatomical and psychophysical evidence puts human hypercolumn spacing at about 1.33–2 mm; with a human V1 of about 3,500 mm² per hemisphere and hypercolumns of about 2.67 mm², about 1,300 hypercolumns. The model assumes all orientations at every position and a continuum, although many hallucination patterns have wavelengths of about twice the hypercolumn spacing.

risk_of_bias.note: No validated instrument exists for a theoretical model; on the card's checklist the comparison with hallucinations is high risk: it is by eye, against a few drawings redrawn from secondary sources (popular-science articles, a petroglyph, cave-art illustrations), with no measure of fit; two premises have no source (that all observers report Klüver's form constants, and the 30 to 40 repetitions that set the expected scale); and the results are sensitive to the assumed lateral connectivity, the contour-forming patterns appearing only with lateral spread wider than the anatomy that motivated the model. The mathematics itself is printed in full.

inconsistency.note: One model; no competing model is developed or compared.

indirectness.note: No measurement in people, and none during drug use: the drug enters only as an abstract rise in excitability or fall in inhibition, the same mechanism the paper offers for flickering light, and the anatomy comes mainly from cats, macaques, owl monkeys and tree shrews (partly unpublished), scaled to human V1.

publication_bias.note: Not applicable to a single theoretical paper.

grade.reasoning: A theoretical model is not evidence from measurement and starts low; rated down one level for risk of bias (the fit to hallucinations judged by eye against a few redrawn images, unsourced premises, sensitivity to the assumed connectivity) and one for indirectness (no human or drug data; the drug as an abstract parameter; animal anatomy), which is below the floor: very low. Worded as insufficient evidence on whether psychedelic geometric visuals arise this way: what the model proposes, what it rests on and what it predicts are reported as such, not rated as findings about the brain. Status single study: one modelling paper; it extends the corresponding author's earlier model (Ermentrout & Cowan, 1979), which is not counted as independent support, and no empirical test of its predictions has been read.

(2000b), to which the fuller stability analysis is deferred; and any study that imaged visual cortex during geometric hallucinations (for example the LSD brain-imaging study named in the demand file, Carhart-Harris et al., 2016), which would be the first test in people.
